cards.title: Filter Ad Spy Tools for Proven, Facebook-Scaled Winners
cards.summary: Exact Get Hooked filter stack for surfacing validated, older-demographic Facebook winners.
cards.use_when: Configuring an ad-spy tool such as Get Hooked to find products that already have proven spend and scale behind them.
steps: Set Location to USA.
Turn on 'Top performing' only, so you see proven winners rather than speculative tests.
Cap results to a maximum of four ads per brand to reduce noise from one advertiser flooding the feed.
Set Format to Video.
Set Status to 'Currently running' so you only see live, funded campaigns.
Set Minimum Runtime to 14 days — the source treats this as the proof of baseline profitability.
Set Channel to Facebook, because the source argues Facebook skews to older, easier-to-convert buyers.
Set Brand Active Ads to greater than 50, indicating high scale and budget.
Try a niche category first; if results are junk or repetitive, turn the niche off and search manual keywords instead (e.g., a specific symptom or condition), because categories misclassify some ads.
Expect this to require hours of scrolling, not a quick pass; the source frames persistence as the actual work.
caveats: Tool interfaces and filter names change; verify the current Get Hooked layout before relying on exact labels.
The 14-day runtime and 50-active-ads thresholds are the presenter's heuristics, not guarantees of profitability.
Niche categories under-include relevant health ads, so manual keyword search is often necessary.

cards.title: Product Criteria: Daily Problem Plus Retail Absence
cards.summary: Two baseline criteria — a problem that recurs daily and no big-box retail availability — for screening product ideas.
cards.use_when: Screening candidate products before spending on creative, site build or inventory, especially in health and wellness.
steps: Check that the product solves a real problem, either a deep emotional problem/desire or a physical problem the buyer feels every single day.
Use the source's example: foot pain — felt every time the person walks — so they will buy almost anything if the copy is good.
Confirm the product is not available in big-box retail stores; retail absence protects margin and ad-driven demand.
Prefer problems with high daily frequency and strong aversion (chronic pain, child sleep disruption, incontinence) because urgency shortens the buying decision.

Assess 'deeply annoying daily problem' as a better signal than 'cool product' — the source explicitly rates a boring problem like tinnitus higher than a gimmicky pillow because of the ongoing irritation.
caveats: Applies to physical problem-solution goods aimed at older buyers; not a universal test for all ecommerce categories.
Retail absence is a margin/protection heuristic, not proof of demand — validate separately with ad intelligence.
The source presents these as his screen, not an empirically benchmarked rule.

cards.title: Native Ad Scouting on News Publisher Widgets
cards.summary: Use paid-content widgets on weather and news sites to surface recurring, older-demographic health offers.
cards.use_when: Sourcing product ideas and native-ad angles aimed at a 60+ audience outside of ad spy tools.
steps: Open a news or weather site with a paid content / sponsored widget block — the source names weather.com and CNN.
Repeatedly refresh the widget to rotate through a new batch of paid placements; the same few offers recurring across refreshes is the signal.
Log the health and wellness categories that keep appearing — the source repeatedly sees neuropathy, tinnitus, bladder control, hearing aids, snoring/sleep apnea, neck pain, hip and knee pain.
Treat candidates that are new stores (little or no visit data shown) as under-advertised opportunities rather than reasons to skip.
Evaluate the problem's severity and privacy sensitivity: the source rates female 60+ bladder incontinence as a strong problem because sufferers strongly want to stop it.
Choose an angle against the problem type, not just the product: for tinnitus, the source argues a supplement could beat an existing pillow offer by going after the underlying irritation.
caveats: Works specifically because older audiences dominate these sites — it is a demographic-targeting tactic, not a general trend feed.
Traffic-estimate tools may show nothing for new or low-traffic stores; absence of data is not absence of demand but also not validation.
Many widgets show low-quality or repeated offers; expect to filter heavily.

cards.title: Cross-Validate With the Free Facebook Ad Library
cards.summary: Use Ad Library image filtering and run-time checks as a free substitute for a paid ad spy tool before committing.
cards.use_when: Validating a shortlisted product and checking whether competitors are already running native-style image ads.
steps: Set the Ad Library country filter to the target market (the source uses USA) and search the product keyword, e.g. 'sleep patch'.
Switch the media filter to Images to surface native-style static ads rather than video.
Confirm the ads have been active for more than about one week; that run time is the source's signal that the offer is converting.

Read the pattern, not one ad: for the child sleep patch example the source found image ads running but judged that almost nobody was actually running native for it, concluding it was an open opportunity.
Treat Ad Library as the free equivalent of Get Hooked — useful when you do not pay for an ad spy subscription, but it requires manual keyword hunting (e.g., 'health', 'pain').
caveats: Ad Library does not expose the performance or engagement metrics a paid spy tool provides; run time is a proxy, not proof.
One week of activity is the presenter's heuristic.
Searching vague keywords produces a lot of irrelevant results and takes longer than filtered spy tools.

cards.title: Mine the Longest-Running Ad for the Winning Angle
cards.summary: Extract the marketing avatar and message from a validated product's longest-running creative and reuse that angle.
cards.use_when: You have a validated product with a history of running ads and need a starting creative angle before building your own.
steps: Open the advertiser's full Facebook page profile for the validated product.
Sort or locate the longest-running ads on that page — persistence is treated as the strongest available evidence of what converts.
Identify the specific avatar being spoken to (e.g., a mother worn down by a four-year-old's bedtime battles) and the exact message framing used in that ad.
Duplicate that avatar and angle when building your own native ad for the same problem.
Use a better-executed version of the same angle rather than inventing a new one, and go deeper on research than the competition when entering a contested problem like neuropathy.
caveats: This is angle mining, not permission to copy creative assets; the source describes replicating the angle and avatar, not the production.
Longest-running ads may still be unprofitable — run time only proves continued spend, not positive ROAS.
In saturated categories (the source names neuropathy), the same angle alone may not be enough; deeper copy research is his stated edge.

cards.title: Prioritize Facebook Over TikTok/Instagram Burner Scouting
cards.summary: Deprioritize TikTok and Instagram burner-account scouting in favor of Facebook-based and tool-based research.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to spend product-research hours, particularly as a beginner without a trained dropshipping eye.
steps: Treat TikTok and Instagram burner-account scrolling as outdated and ineffective for finding winners, per the source.

Recognize that burner methods work only with a trained 'dropshipping eye', which the source says takes 3–6 months to develop, and that Instagram burners largely repost content from TikTok or AliExpress.
If you still want a burner method, use a Facebook burner account: the source says it surfaces the older demographic and is a decent research surface.
Replace burner scrolling with the three 2026 methods: native scouting, a paid ad spy tool (Get Hooked), and the free Ad Library.
Avoid ripping a product from a crowded sourcing feed: the source argues you learn no skill, cannot replicate the win, and face high CPMs/CPCs because 'thousands' of people work the same feed daily.
caveats: This is the presenter's opinion and is tied to his stated 2026 timeframe; platform behavior changes.
The criticism applies to learning quality and saturation, not to whether winning products exist on those platforms at all.
A trained eye is presented as a prerequisite for burner methods, so beginners are the group most disadvantaged by them.
